source.title: Erasing Without Remembering: Safeguarding Knowledge Forgetting in Large Language Models
source.authors: Hua-Zheng Wang; Yong-Cheng Jing; Hai-Feng Sun; Ying-Jie Wang; Jing-Yu Wang; Jian-Xin Liao; Da-Cheng Tao

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. There are some flattened table layouts and figure-only results, but no apparent truncation.
record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates whether unlearning generalizes to rephrased prompts and probes whether target-answer information remains represented across model layers. It uses its own datasets and metrics rather than reproducing the original sources’ attack protocols.
record.gate_note: The paper tests rephrased-question and paraphrased-answer recall after unlearning, plus layerwise answer-token ranks. It does not test recovery by post-unlearning fine-tuning, activation ablation, or quantization. The paper’s layer and token-sensitivity values used to choose perturbations are not treated as results here. Results cited from other work are excluded.
record.test_reason: The study measures residual target knowledge after 15 unlearning methods on TOFU, Harry Potter and ZsRE. It uses its own metrics: forget probability on original and rephrased questions, paraphrased-answer probability, and layerwise answer-token rank. These bear on whether unlearning works (A), whether rephrasing exposes knowledge (E), and whether internal layers retain it (C). It also proposes PERMU and evaluates it on the same rephrased and layerwise tests (F). It does not reproduce the originals' attack protocols.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that existing methods forget only the exact unlearning samples: paraphrased answers remain probable and the correct answer re-emerges in middle layers, so knowledge is not fully erased. PERMU improves forgetting on original and rephrased data while keeping utility, but forgetting one-hop and other logically related knowledge remains poor for all methods.
record.recipe_differences: This is a broad evaluation of 15 unlearning methods and a new method, PERMU, on TOFU, Harry Potter, ZsRE, WMDP, and MUSE. It tests paraphrased and logically related samples rather than reproducing the original studies’ attack protocols.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that results vary across datasets, model scales, forget-set sizes, and perturbation settings. Its discussion says one-hop reasoning remains especially difficult; PERMU’s forgetting/utility trade-off changes with K, P, and C.

fits_no_version.finding: ZsRE relation-reversed, subject-replaced and one-hop questions keep high F1/ROUGE after all unlearning methods, with one-hop hardest; DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B forgets one-hop somewhat better.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Unlearning does not propagate to logically related facts (reversal, alias, one-hop).

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The paper reports averages over three runs but no error bars or other uncertainty estimates. It does not calibrate its forgetting metrics against chance. The cited retain model is a reference trained without the forget set, not a chance-level baseline. Internal-layer evidence is shown in figures without numerical layerwise values, and the study does not test the proposed fine-tuning, ablation, or quantization attacks.
record.rows_left_out: Table 2’s reported delta column and table metrics other than Forget Probability in Table 4 were omitted because they are not separate direct recovery measures for the selected rows. Table 4 results for ICL, ECO, and regularized GA/DPO/NPO variants were omitted under the 60-row cap. Tables 5–18 include other datasets, transformations, PERMU ablations, utility, fluency, and computational results; they were not included because they do not directly measure the selected prompt-recovery or internal-layer claim, or are comparisons of the new method rather than the claim’s attack objects.

untested.parts: Chance-level or multiple-choice accuracy (as in WMDP), and recovery attacks other than rephrasing and related-fact queries.
Entire version: no relearning or fine-tuning attack.
Activation-direction ablation; only logit-lens style rank analysis is done, on GA only.
Jailbreaks, other languages, and in-context information. Rephrasing is tested, but direct-prompt forgetting was weak, so recovery cannot be isolated.
PERMU's resistance to fine-tuning, ablation, quantization, jailbreak or multilingual attacks.

missing.what: Harry Potter forget and rephrased-forget F1/ROUGE for all methods on Phi-1.3B and LLaMA2-7B. On LLaMA2-7B, rephrased F1 is about 82–97 vs retain 36.4. This bears on A and shows rephrased roughly equals original. Declared left out, but the exclusion reason is wrong: it does directly measure rephrased recall.
ULD qualitative case: on the original question ULD answers 'travelogue'; on the rephrased question it gives the true 'French literature'.

PERMU tuning coefficient C sweep on Phi-1.3B Forget01. At C=0.4, forget Pr is 0.83 and rephrased Pr 0.88, but MU falls from 50.50 to 31.85. PERMU's robustness depends on hyperparameters and costs utility.

Original-sample forget probability for Forget01 and Forget10 (LLaMA2-7B baselines), needed to judge whether rephrasing raises recall. It is not reported, so this is a gap in the paper rather than in the rows.

record.verdict_notes: Key caveat: at the paper's utility-matched settings, baselines barely forget even the original TOFU Forget05 samples (forget probability 80–98 vs retain 14.6). Their rephrased-question forget probabilities are lower than their original-question ones (e.g. GA 83.41 to 60.21). The study therefore shows weak unlearning and residual knowledge (challenging A), not recovery by rephrasing of knowledge that direct prompts had suppressed. Table 4 rows were relinked from E to A for this reason. PERMU rows evaluate the authors' own method and are kept only for F. The retain model is a never-exposed reference, not chance. Results are averaged over three runs with no uncertainty reported.

versions.untested_parts: The study evaluates forgetting and retained utility, but does not report chance-level accuracy or test whether attacks other than rephrasing recover knowledge.
No post-unlearning fine-tuning or relearning attack is applied.
It probes answer-token ranks across layers, but does not ablate an activation direction or directly establish that knowledge has been deleted rather than made inaccessible.
Rephrased questions and paraphrased answers are tested; jailbreaks, other languages, and in-context recovery information are not.
PERMU is evaluated on rephrased prompts and paraphrased answers, but not on fine-tuning, activation-ablation, quantization, jailbreak, or multilingual attacks.
